cluster_name: Nepal-Tibet glacier flash floods kill over 600, thousands missing
event_summary: A glacial collapse triggered devastating flash floods and landslides along the Nepal-Tibet border on August 27, 2026, killing at least 675 people in Nepal and seven in Tibet, with nearly 3,000 still missing three days later and over 100 workers trapped inside hydropower tunnels.
tldr: The most revealing editorial split in this corpus is geographic: Western outlets consistently label the disaster 'Nepal-Tibet floods', while Pakistani, Turkish, and Nigerian outlets say 'Nepal-China floods', and Russian and Chinese state media refer only to 'Nepal' or 'northern Nepal' — erasing Tibet from the dateline entirely. CGTN's successive dispatches filed death tolls of 157 and then 469, substantially below Nepal's own disaster authority figure of 675+, leaving Tibet-side casualties opaque in state-managed international coverage. Canada's Globe and Mail and South Korea's KBS World domesticated the story by foregrounding their own nationals among the missing, converting a regional mass-casualty event into a consular affairs dispatch for domestic audiences. Across opposing editorial traditions — RT, CGTN, NPR, DW, and regional press alike — the core framing converges on factual humanitarian loss-of-life, making this a rare story where geopolitical spin is absent even from outlets that routinely apply it.

single_outlet_findings.finding: Filed successive reports with death tolls of 157 and then 469, substantially below Nepal's disaster authority figure of 675+; refers only to 'northern Nepal' without mentioning Tibet, erasing the cross-border dimension from the dateline.

Labels the disaster 'Nepal floods' with no Tibet qualifier, and reports 'China has confirmed 3 deaths' — a figure far below the 7 Tibet-side deaths cited by AFP — without editorial comment on the discrepancy.
Headlines the disaster as 'Nepal, China floods', co-billing China as a primary affected party rather than using the 'Nepal-Tibet' framing common to Western outlets.
Also labels the story 'Nepal, China floods', joining Pakistan's ARY News in treating China as co-equal to Nepal rather than referencing Tibet as a geographic qualifier.
Runs two separate articles: one leading with 25 Canadian nationals among the missing, the other tracking the rising death toll — the most domesticated coverage in the corpus.
Explicitly attributes the disaster to 'a glacier collapse', the only outlet to name glacial collapse as the cause in its body text, implicitly inviting a climate-attribution reading.

Describes surveillance footage from 'the Chinese side of the frontier' showing a massive mud wall — the only outlet to cite Chinese-side visual evidence, framing the Tibet angle without invoking sovereignty language.
Publishes satellite imagery showing the full scale of destruction, positioning the story through aerial visual evidence rather than rescue operations or death toll counts alone.

bottom_line: The Nepal-Tibet flood story split along geographic naming lines that track editorial independence: Western outlets said 'Nepal-Tibet', Pakistani, Turkish, and Nigerian outlets said 'Nepal-China', and Russian and Chinese state media referred only to 'Nepal' or 'northern Nepal', erasing Tibet from the dateline entirely. CGTN's early death-toll dispatches (157, then 469) ran substantially below Nepal's own disaster authority (675+), leaving the Tibet-side casualty picture unresolved in international coverage while the rest of the press converged on factual humanitarian framing.
